doctrines/theological-schools/question: How should Christians do theology, and what are the great schools that have tried?
doctrines/theological-schools/summary: Christians agree that theology is "faith seeking understanding", but disagree about how: by prayerful reading of Scripture, by rigorous reasoning, by confessional system, by reflection on religious experience, or from the experience of the poor and the margins. This map traces the great schools from Alexandria and Antioch through monastic and scholastic theology, Thomism, Scotism and nominalism, humanism, Protestant orthodoxy, Puritanism and Pietism, the Enlightenment and liberalism, to neo-orthodoxy, existentialism, neo-patristic and ressourcement theology, postliberalism, Radical Orthodoxy and the contextual, liberation and Pentecostal theologies of world Christianity.
doctrines/theological-schools/longText:
Every Christian theology answers, explicitly or not, a question of method: where does knowledge of God come from, and how should it be put into words? Scripture is the common starting point, but already in the 3rd century Christians disagreed about how to read it. The Alexandrian teachers Clement and Origen, at home in Platonism, sought spiritual senses beneath the letter; the Antiochenes Diodore, Theodore and John Chrysostom insisted on history and grammar. Tertullian asked what Athens had to do with Jerusalem, while Augustine taught the West to "believe in order to understand", a formula Anselm made the programme of medieval thought.

In the 12th century two styles of theology diverged. Monastic theology, exemplified by Bernard of Clairvaux, treated theology as prayerful savouring of Scripture; the new urban schools, led by Abelard and Peter Lombard, posed questions, compared authorities and resolved them by logic. Bernard secured Abelard’s condemnation in 1141, yet the scholastic method won the universities. Thomas Aquinas integrated Aristotle into a synthesis in which grace perfects nature; Duns Scotus and the Franciscans stressed divine freedom and love; William of Ockham and the via moderna separated what reason can prove from what faith receives and framed salvation as God’s covenant. Luther, trained in this nominalism, rejected scholastic theology as a whole, while Renaissance humanists called everyone back "to the sources".

The Reformation churches soon produced their own scholasticism, the Lutheran and Reformed orthodoxy of Gerhard, Turretin and Owen, while English Puritans and German Pietists insisted that theology be practical and lived. The Enlightenment made reason the judge of revelation, and Deists reduced Christianity to natural religion. Friedrich Schleiermacher answered by grounding theology in religious experience, inaugurating liberal Protestantism, which Ritschl and Harnack turned toward history and ethics and the social gospel toward society. The First World War discredited that synthesis for Karl Barth, whose dialectical theology insisted on God’s self-revelation; his 1923 exchange with Harnack crystallised the clash. Bultmann and Tillich took the existentialist road; Orthodox theologians in exile (Florovsky, Lossky) called for a neo-patristic synthesis; French Catholics (de Lubac, Congar) returned to the Fathers against the neo-Thomist manuals that Leo XIII had made official in 1879, and were vindicated at Vatican II.

Since the 1960s, theologians have asked whose experience theology reflects. Latin American liberation theology, Black theology (James Cone), feminist and womanist theology, African theology (Mbiti, Bediako, Oduyoye), Asian minjung, Dalit and contextual theologies and, increasingly, Pentecostal theology (Amos Yong) speak from contexts once ignored. Postliberals (Lindbeck, Hauerwas) and Radical Orthodoxy (Milbank) challenged the very idea of neutral foundations, while evangelical, process and confessional theologies continue their own traditions. The atlas presents each school in its own best terms and with its critics; none is declared the right method.
doctrines/theological-schools/flow/nodes: How should Christians do theology, and what are the great schools that have tried?

Is theology prayerful wisdom, rigorous science, confessional teaching, reflection on experience, or speech from the margins? How do Scripture, tradition, reason, experience and context relate, and why have Christians formed rival schools of method?
Luke 24:27: "beginning at Moses and all the prophets"
The risen Christ interprets "in all the scriptures the things concerning himself": the root of Christological reading of the Old Testament, claimed by literal and spiritual exegetes alike.
Acts 17 and Colossians 2:8: engaging and resisting philosophy
Paul quotes Greek poets at Athens (Acts 17:28) yet warns against "philosophy and vain deceit" (Col 2:8). Every school has had to decide how much the wisdom of the world may serve theology.
Galatians 4:24: "which things are an allegory"
Paul reads Sarah and Hagar as two covenants and the Exodus as a type for the Church (1 Cor 10), licensing figurative reading.
Tertullian: "What has Athens to do with Jerusalem?"
Against Gnostic speculation Tertullian rejects a "Stoic, Platonic and dialectic Christianity", though he himself used philosophy and law with skill.
Alexandria: philosophy and the spiritual sense
Clement and Origen treat philosophy as a schoolmaster to Christ and read Scripture at several levels, seeking its spiritual sense.
Antioch: history, grammar and theoria
Diodore, Theodore and Chrysostom insist on the historical sense, using typology but resisting allegory.
Augustine: believe in order to understand
Augustine makes faith the door to understanding and, in On Christian Teaching, lets the rule of love govern interpretation, a synthesis the West inherited.
Constantinople II (553) condemns Theodore and Origenist teachings

The council condemns the person and writings of Theodore of Mopsuestia among the Three Chapters, and in the same period Origenist speculations are anathematised; the Church of the East continues to honour Theodore.
Anselm: faith seeking understanding
At Bec, Anselm prays and reasons his way to proofs of God’s existence and the necessity of the incarnation, a bridge from cloister to school.
Monastic theology: knowledge through love
Bernard and the Cistercians practise theology as prayerful savouring of Scripture rather than disputation.
Council of Sens condemns Abelard (1141)
Bernard of Clairvaux attacks Abelard’s dialectic as presumptuous; propositions from his works are condemned and confirmed by Innocent II.
Scholastic method: questions, authorities, distinctions
Abelard’s Sic et Non and Peter Lombard’s Sentences give the universities their method and textbook.
Aquinas: grace perfects nature
Thomas Aquinas integrates Aristotle into a theology in which reason and revelation form a harmonious whole.
Paris condemnations of 1277
Bishop Tempier condemns 219 propositions of radical Aristotelianism, affirming God’s absolute freedom and casting a shadow over some Thomist theses.
Scotus: univocity, will and the primacy of Christ
The Franciscan school stresses divine freedom and love and challenges Thomist analogy.
Ockham and the via moderna
Nominalists separate what reason can demonstrate from what faith receives and frame salvation as God’s covenant.
Humanism: back to the sources
Erasmus’s Greek New Testament and the call ad fontes challenge scholastic method and fuel reform on all sides.
Luther against scholastic theology
Trained in the via moderna, Luther attacks Aristotle’s role in theology and calls for a theology of the cross grounded in Scripture.
Puritan practical divinity
Perkins and his heirs apply Reformed doctrine to conscience and daily life.
Protestant scholasticism
Lutheran and Reformed orthodoxy systematise the Reformation in loci and disputations, using scholastic tools.
Pietism: from correct doctrine to living faith
Spener and Francke call theology back to new birth, Bible study and practice.
Enlightenment rationalism and Deism
Reason becomes judge of revelation; Toland, Tindal and later Kant reduce Christianity toward natural and moral religion.
Schleiermacher: theology from religious experience
Schleiermacher grounds theology in the feeling of absolute dependence; Ritschl and Harnack shape a historical, ethical liberalism, and the social gospel follows.
Theology in the modern research university

With the University of Berlin (1810) and Schleiermacher’s Brief Outline (1811), theology is reorganised as a historical and practical academic discipline, separating biblical, historical, systematic and practical fields, a model copied worldwide.
Aeterni Patris (1879) enthrones Thomism
Leo XIII makes Aquinas the norm for Catholic philosophy and theology, launching neo-scholasticism.
Barth and dialectical theology
After 1914 Barth’s Romans proclaims the "wholly other" God known only in his self-revelation, breaking with liberalism.
Barth versus Harnack (1923)
Teacher and pupil debate in print whether theology is a historical science accountable to general reason, or obedient witness to the Word of God.
Orthodox neo-patristic synthesis
Florovsky and Lossky call Orthodox theology back to the mind of the Fathers, uniting dogma and mystical experience.
Existentialist theology: Bultmann and Tillich
Demythologising and the method of correlation translate the gospel into the existential questions of modern people.
Nouvelle théologie and ressourcement
De Lubac, Congar and others return to the Fathers and liturgy against neo-scholastic manuals; censured in 1950, vindicated at Vatican II.
Vatican II (1962-65) adopts ressourcement
The Council’s texts on revelation, liturgy and the Church draw on ressourcement theologians and end the monopoly of neo-scholastic manuals.
Theologies from the margins: Black, feminist, liberation
Cone’s Black theology (1969), Gutiérrez’s liberation theology (1971) and feminist and womanist theology make the experience of the oppressed a starting point of method.
Postliberalism and Radical Orthodoxy
Lindbeck’s cultural-linguistic model (1984) and Milbank’s critique of secular reason (1990) reject both liberal and rationalist foundations for theology.
World Christianity: African, Asian and Pentecostal theologies
With most Christians now in the Global South, theologians such as Mbiti, Bediako, Oduyoye, Koyama, Song and Yong argue that theology must be done in many tongues and cultures.
Today: many schools, one question of method

Neo-Thomists, Reformed and Lutheran retrievalists, evangelicals, Orthodox neo-patristic theologians, process, liberation, Pentecostal and contextual theologians coexist; the old debate about faith, reason, experience and context continues across all of them.
doctrines/spirituality-prayer/name: Spirituality, prayer and the spiritual life
doctrines/spirituality-prayer/question: How do Christians pray and seek union with God, and which ways of the spiritual life are faithful?
doctrines/spirituality-prayer/summary: From the Desert Fathers to Korean dawn prayer, Christians have developed many schools of prayer: monastic rule and lectio divina, the Jesus Prayer of the hesychasts, Franciscan and Rhineland mysticism, the Devotio Moderna, Ignatian discernment and Carmelite contemplation, Puritan meditation, Pietist heart religion, Quaker silence, Wesley’s means of grace, Keswick surrender, Pentecostal tongues and the modern contemplative revival. Alongside them run perennial disputes: mysticism versus Word-centred piety, monastic asceticism versus vocation in the world, the invocation of saints, and whether contemplative techniques are biblical.
doctrines/spirituality-prayer/longText:
Christian prayer begins with the Psalms and with Jesus’ teaching: pray in secret, say "Our Father", do not heap up empty phrases, and pray always. Paul spoke of being caught up to the third heaven and of believers beholding the Lord’s glory and being transformed. From these seeds grew a remarkable variety of spiritual traditions.

In late-3rd-century Egypt, Antony and the Desert Fathers and Mothers sought God through solitude, fasting, manual work and the guidance of elders; Evagrius and Cassian systematised their wisdom, and Benedict’s Rule (c.530) shaped Western monastic life around the Office, sacred reading and work. Irish and British monks joined severe asceticism to mission. In the East, the practice of repeating the name of Jesus in stillness became hesychasm, defended by Gregory Palamas and upheld by councils at Constantinople (1341, 1351). In the medieval West, Guigo II defined lectio divina, Francis of Assisi embraced poverty and creation, the Rhineland Dominicans preached detachment and the birth of God in the soul (Eckhart’s propositions were condemned in 1329), anchoresses such as Julian of Norwich recorded visions of divine love, and the Devotio Moderna produced The Imitation of Christ.

The Reformation challenged much of this. Luther and Calvin rejected monastic vows, ladders of ascent and the invocation of saints, grounding prayer in the Word and Christ’s sole mediation, yet Protestants soon developed their own disciplines: Puritan meditation, Pietist and Moravian heart religion (with Herrnhut’s hundred-year prayer watch from 1727), Quaker silent worship and Wesley’s methodical use of the means of grace. Catholic reform produced Ignatius’s Spiritual Exercises and the Carmelite mysticism of Teresa of Ávila and John of the Cross, while Rome condemned quietism (1687, 1699). The Orthodox Philokalia (1782) and the Russian elders made the Jesus Prayer available to lay people.

Modern movements have multiplied the options. The Keswick convention (1875) taught a rest of faith; Korean believers have prayed together before dawn since 1906, and African prayer churches and revivals made all-night prayer central; Pentecostal and charismatic Christians pray in tongues and for healing; Thomas Merton and the Centering Prayer movement revived contemplative silence, drawing both enthusiasm and critique (including a 1989 Vatican letter on Christian meditation and many evangelical objections). The atlas presents each school in the words of its practitioners, then the objections of others, without ranking them.
doctrines/spirituality-prayer/flow/nodes: How do Christians pray and seek union with God, and which ways of the spiritual life are faithful?

Christians are told to pray without ceasing and promised that the pure in heart will see God. But should one seek God in solitude or in the world, through Scripture or beyond words, through set methods or spontaneous outpouring, through saints’ prayers or Christ alone? Every tradition has answered with its own school of prayer.
Psalm 1:2 and Psalm 46:10: meditate day and night; be still
The Psalter (compiled over centuries, completed in the Persian period) gives Jews and Christians their prayer book: meditation on the law, lament, praise and stillness before God.
Matthew 6:5-13: pray in secret; the Lord’s Prayer; no vain repetitions
Jesus teaches secret prayer, gives the Our Father and warns against heaping up empty phrases, texts invoked both for and against repetitive prayer.
1 Thessalonians 5:17 and Luke 18:13: pray without ceasing; "God be merciful to me a sinner"
Paul’s command and the tax collector’s plea become the seed of the Jesus Prayer and of unceasing prayer in East and West.
2 Corinthians 12:2-4 and 3:18: caught up to the third heaven; beholding his glory
Paul’s rapture and the promise of transformation "from glory to glory" are foundational for Christian mystical theology, though Paul refuses to boast of visions.
The desert: Antony and the abbas and ammas
Antony’s withdrawal (c.270) and the communities of Egypt make the desert the school of prayer, watchfulness and humility.
Evagrius: the theologian is one who prays truly
Evagrius systematises desert wisdom: the eight thoughts, dispassion and imageless pure prayer.
Augustine: "our heart is restless until it rest in thee"
The Confessions turn autobiography into prayer and make desire for God the engine of the spiritual life in the West.
Benedict’s Rule: prayer, reading and work
The Rule orders a day of Office, lectio divina and labour under an abbot, the backbone of Western monasticism.
Celtic monastic spirituality
Columba’s Iona and the Irish monks combine severe asceticism, pilgrimage, blessing prayers and mission.
Lectio divina: the ladder of reading, meditation, prayer, contemplation
Guigo II formulates the monastic practice of sacred reading in four rungs.
Francis: poverty, creation and the crucified
Francis and his brothers embrace poverty and praise God through all creatures; his stigmata (1224) seal a spirituality of the cross.
Eckhart and the Rhineland mystics
German Dominicans preach detachment and the birth of God in the ground of the soul.
In agro dominico (1329): Eckhart’s propositions condemned
John XXII condemns 28 propositions drawn from Eckhart’s works, a warning to speculative mysticism.
Hesychasm and the Jesus Prayer
On Athos, Gregory Palamas defends monks who pray the Jesus Prayer in stillness and see the uncreated light.
Councils of Constantinople uphold Palamas (1341, 1351)
The Byzantine Church vindicates hesychast prayer and the essence-energies distinction against Barlaam and Akindynos.
Julian of Norwich: "all shall be well"
An English anchoress records sixteen showings of divine love, a witness of mystical experience from within an enclosed parish life.
Devotio Moderna and The Imitation of Christ
Lay brothers and sisters in the Low Countries cultivate methodical, Christ-centred inward devotion.
Reformers: faith comes by hearing, not by ascent
Luther and Calvin reject ladders of mystical ascent, monastic vows and saints’ invocation in favour of prayer grounded in the Word and offered through Christ alone.
Should we ask the saints to pray for us?
The Augsburg Confession (art. 21) and Calvin reject invocation of saints; Catholics, Orthodox and Oriental Orthodox defend it as fellowship with the communion of saints.
Monasteries dissolved in Protestant lands
Reformers redirect asceticism into everyday vocation; England dissolves its monasteries (1536-40). Catholic reform responds with new orders.
Ignatius: the Spiritual Exercises and discernment
The Exercises teach imaginative Gospel contemplation and the discernment of spirits for decisions and mission.
Teresa and John: the interior castle and the dark night
The Carmelite reformers map the soul’s journey to union through prayer and purifying darkness.
Puritan meditation and the practice of piety
Baxter and others teach daily Scripture meditation, secret prayer and self-examination.
Quaker silence: waiting on the inward light
Fox’s Friends worship in expectant silence without liturgy or clergy.
Quietism condemned (1687, 1699)
Rome condemns Molinos’s passive prayer of quiet and later Fénelon’s Maxims; Catholic authorities grow wary of mystical prayer.
Pietist and Moravian heart religion
Herrnhut’s Pentecost (1727) launches a century of continuous prayer and mission centred on love for the crucified Saviour.
Wesley: the means of grace
Against Moravian "stillness", Wesley teaches that prayer, Scripture and the Lord’s Supper are ordinary channels of grace on the way to perfect love.
The Philokalia and the Russian elders
Nicodemus and Macarius publish the hesychast anthology; Paisius, Seraphim of Sarov, Optina and the Way of a Pilgrim spread the Jesus Prayer.
Keswick: the rest of faith
The Higher Life movement teaches surrender and abiding as the secret of the victorious Christian life.
Korean dawn prayer and African prayer movements
Daily dawn prayer from Pyongyang (1906-07), prayer mountains, Aladura vigils and the East African Revival make corporate prayer the engine of growth.
Pentecostal and charismatic prayer
Praying in tongues, prayer for healing and expectant worship spread from Azusa Street to the historic churches through the charismatic renewal.
Merton and Centering Prayer
Trappists and others offer the contemplative tradition to lay Christians; Protestants join through the spiritual formation movement.
Is contemplative prayer biblical? Cautions and critiques
The CDF’s 1989 letter and evangelical critics warn against mind-emptying techniques and borrowing from non-Christian meditation; contemplatives answer that their sources are Christian.
Global prayer today: vigils, prayer mountains and 24-7 prayer
Most praying Christians now live in the Global South, where all-night vigils, prayer camps and Pentecostal worship are normal; 24-hour prayer movements have spread worldwide.
Today: an ecumenical exchange of spiritual practices

Evangelicals practise lectio divina and silence, Catholics join charismatic prayer, Orthodox prayer ropes and Taizé chants cross borders, while debates continue about mysticism, technique, saints and Scripture.
